headline: A waist check may help doctors find obesity

sources.title: BMI alternative for identifying obesity 'could prevent misdiagnosis in millions' (The Guardian)
Move over BMI: new obesity definition is better for predicting your health (Nature)
New clinical definition outperforms BMI in diagnosing obesity (King's College London, EurekAlert!)

chunks.text: Two people can have the same [[body mass index]] but very different health. This index is a number made from weight and height. Doctors use it to find [[obesity]], or too much [[body fat]]. But the index {{leaves out}} where the fat sits. People with lots of [[muscle]] or lots of fat can get the same high number. A study in the [[journal]] Nature, published on November 11, 2026, says a [[waist]] check can help doctors {{tell these people apart}}.

verbs.why: My little brother leaves out the onions when he makes soup. The short version of the movie leaves out two scenes. The body mass index alone leaves out where a person's fat sits.

verbs.correct: To see how two people or things differ
verbs.wrong: To weigh two people at the same time
verbs.why: Many parents tell their twins apart by their voices. A good cook tells fresh fish and old fish apart by the smell. A study says a waist check can help doctors tell people with muscle and people with fat apart.

chunks.text: An international group of obesity experts {{came up with}} this new method in January 2025. It keeps the index but adds two [[measurements]]: waist size, and waist size compared with height. Experts say fat that {{builds up}} around the [[belly]] is linked to more [[health problems]]. Researchers {{looked into}} the method using the [[health records]] of 844,108 adults in China, Britain, the U.S. and Spain.

verbs.correct: To create a new idea or plan
verbs.wrong: To forget an old idea or plan
verbs.why: Our team comes up with a new name for the club every year. My son comes up with funny stories at dinner. In January 2025, an international group of obesity experts came up with a new way to find obesity.
Dust builds up under the bed. Snow builds up on the roof in winter. Experts say fat that builds up around the belly is linked to more health problems.
The police look into every report of a stolen car. The school looks into all complaints from parents. Researchers looked into the method using the health records of 844,108 adults in four countries.

chunks.text: The index alone did not {{pick up}} obesity in as many as 9 percent of people. It wrongly [[labeled]] as many as 3 percent as having obesity. A [[surgeon]] at King's College London who helped create the method said these mistakes can {{add up to}} [[tens of millions]] of people. For people with obesity, a higher [[risk of death]] {{showed up}} only when waist size was added.

verbs.why: A good doctor picks up small changes in a patient's voice. This test picks up problems early. The body mass index alone did not pick up obesity in as many as 9 percent of people.
Small daily costs add up to a lot of money. Ten minutes of walking each day adds up to more than an hour a week. A surgeon said the mistakes can add up to tens of millions of people.

verbs.correct: To appear or become easy to see
verbs.wrong: To stay the same for years
verbs.why: Spots show up on the skin after a day in the sun. Mistakes show up when you read your work aloud. For people with obesity, a higher risk of death showed up only when waist size was added.

chunks.text: The method {{breaks obesity down}} into two levels. In clinical obesity, extra fat is already harming the [[organs]]. In pre-clinical obesity, the fat is a [[health risk]], but the organs still work. Within 10 years, 77 to 91 percent of people with pre-clinical obesity did not {{end up}} with clinical obesity. The surgeon said this level should not be {{brushed off}} as [[harmless]] or treated [[automatically]] as a disease. A Chinese researcher on the study said the results {{back up}} the idea of using the method [[worldwide]].

verbs.correct: To make smaller groups from something
verbs.wrong: To give something a new name
verbs.why: The teacher breaks the class down into four teams. The report breaks the costs down into food, rent and travel. The new method breaks obesity down into two levels.

verbs.correct: To reach a certain situation at last
verbs.wrong: To be tested again by a doctor
verbs.why: People who skip breakfast often end up hungry before lunch. Many students end up with jobs in other cities. Most people with pre-clinical obesity did not end up with clinical obesity within 10 years.

verbs.correct: To treat something as not important
verbs.wrong: To test something in a lab
verbs.why: My boss never brushes off my questions. Some people brush off a bad cough for weeks. The surgeon said pre-clinical obesity should not be brushed off as harmless.

verbs.correct: To support an idea with facts
verbs.wrong: To ask people to change a plan
verbs.why: Good writers back up their opinions with numbers. Photos often back up a driver's story after a crash. A Chinese researcher on the study said the results back up the idea of using the method around the world.

ex: Please don't leave out any names from the list.
He left out the sugar, so the cake tasted strange.
The news report left out an important detail.

vocab.def: To see how two people or things differ
ex: I can't tell the two sisters apart in photos.
It is hard to tell real money and fake money apart.
Can you tell these two songs apart?

vocab.def: To create a new idea or plan
ex: She came up with a great idea for the party.
We need to come up with a plan before Monday.
He came up with a new recipe for chicken soup.
Ice built up on the car windows overnight.
Water can build up in the garden after heavy rain.
Old papers built up on her desk for months.
The city will look into the noise problem.
My bank is looking into a strange charge on my card.
We asked the landlord to look into the broken heater.
The camera picked up a fox in the yard at night.
Did you pick up anything strange in his voice?
Dogs can pick up smells that people miss.
All those coffees add up to a big bill each month.
Her small savings add up to enough for a new laptop.
The extra hours add up to two full days of work.

vocab.def: To appear or become easy to see
ex: The crack only shows up in bright light.
Her name didn't show up on the list.
Problems with the engine showed up after the long trip.

vocab.def: To make smaller groups from something
ex: Let's break the project down into small steps.
The bill breaks down the price of each part.
The survey breaks the answers down by age group.

vocab.def: To reach a certain situation at last
ex: We got lost and ended up in the wrong town.
If you don't study, you could end up failing the test.
She ended up as a teacher, not a lawyer.

vocab.def: To treat something as not important
ex: He brushed off the pain in his knee for a month.
Don't brush off advice from your doctor.
She brushed off the question with a smile.

vocab.def: To support an idea with facts
ex: Can you back up that claim with facts?
The numbers back up what the teacher said.
New tests backed up the first results.

wordDefs.def: A number made from your weight and height
ex: The nurse wrote my body mass index on the chart.
An online tool can tell you your body mass index.
Her body mass index is normal for her height.

wordDefs.def: The condition of having too much body fat
ex: Obesity is more common in some countries than others.
The school wants to fight child obesity with more sports.
Doctors talk about obesity with care and respect.

wordDefs.def: The fat that a body stores under the skin and around organs
ex: Some gyms have a machine that measures body fat.
Runners often have very little body fat.
A healthy diet can lower body fat over time.

wordDefs.def: The parts of the body that help you move and lift things
ex: He has a lot of muscle from working on a farm.
Swimming builds muscle in your arms and back.
Cycling builds muscle in your legs.

wordDefs.def: The middle part of the body, above the hips
ex: These pants are too tight around the waist.
She tied a sweater around her waist.
The nurse measures his waist with a tape measure.

wordDefs.def: A magazine that prints new science or medical studies
ex: My doctor reads a medical journal every month.
The scientists sent their study to a journal.
A science journal printed her report on bees.

wordDefs.def: Numbers that show the size or amount of something
ex: The tailor took my measurements for a new suit.
Write down the measurements of the window before you buy curtains.
The nurse checked her measurements at every visit.

wordDefs.def: The front part of the body below the chest
ex: The baby laughed when I touched her belly.
My belly hurts after I eat too fast.
The dog likes to sleep on its belly.

wordDefs.def: Illnesses or conditions that make a person less healthy
ex: Smoking can lead to serious health problems.
My grandfather has a few health problems, but he still walks every day.
Stress can cause health problems at work.

wordDefs.def: Official notes about a person's illnesses and medical care
ex: The new clinic asked for my health records.
Patients can see their health records online.
Health records must be kept private.

wordDefs.def: Called or described as a certain kind of thing
ex: The quiet student was labeled shy by his classmates.
The food was labeled healthy, but it had lots of sugar.
She was unfairly labeled a bad driver.

wordDefs.def: A very large number, more than 20 million
ex: Tens of millions of people watched the final game.
The company lost tens of millions of dollars.
The song was played tens of millions of times online.

wordDefs.def: The chance that a person will die
ex: Wearing a seat belt lowers the risk of death in a crash.
Smoking raises the risk of death from heart disease.
Doctors try to lower the risk of death during surgery.

wordDefs.def: A doctor who does operations on the body
ex: The surgeon fixed my broken arm with a metal plate.
My aunt is a heart surgeon at a big hospital.
The surgeon talked to the family after the operation.

wordDefs.def: Body parts such as the heart, liver and lungs that do special jobs
ex: The heart and lungs are important organs.
Some people agree to give their organs after they die.
Too much alcohol can harm your organs.

wordDefs.def: Something that may cause illness in the future
ex: Sitting all day is a health risk.
Dirty water is a big health risk for children.
Doctors say poor sleep is a health risk.

wordDefs.def: In every case, without checking first
ex: Don't automatically believe everything you read online.
The store does not automatically give refunds.
She automatically said yes to every request.

wordDefs.def: In every part of the world
ex: The singer has fans worldwide.
The company sells its phones worldwide.
Coffee is popular worldwide.

wordDefs.def: Not able to cause any damage or pain
ex: The spider looks scary, but it is harmless.
It was a harmless joke, and everyone laughed.
Most mushrooms in the park are harmless, but don't eat them.

mainIdea.s: A study found that adding a waist check to the usual weight and height number helps doctors find obesity more accurately. It also showed that extra fat harms the organs in only some people.
mainIdea.why: The usual number alone did not pick up obesity in many people. The new method breaks obesity down into two levels, and only clinical obesity already harms organs.

mainIdea.s: Scientists now say doctors should stop using the old weight and height number and measure only the waist. They found that everyone with a large waist is already sick and needs treatment now.
mainIdea.why: Close, but the new method keeps the body mass index and adds waist size. Most people with pre-clinical obesity did not end up with clinical obesity within 10 years.

mainIdea.s: A city in Europe has opened new parks and bike lanes to help children stay active after school. Local leaders and parents hope that more outdoor play will keep young people at a healthy weight.
mainIdea.why: This is about a better way to find obesity. Researchers looked into the health records of 844,108 adults and tested a method that adds a waist check.

tf.s: People with the same body mass index can have very different health.
tf.why: A person with a lot of muscle can have a high number and little fat, and a waist check helps doctors tell these people apart.

tf.s: The body mass index alone picked up obesity in every person in the study.
tf.why: It did not pick up obesity in as many as 9 percent of people, and it wrongly labeled as many as 3 percent.

tf.s: Obesity's link to a higher risk of death showed up when waist size was used.
tf.why: For people with obesity, the higher risk of death showed up only when waist size was used, not with the body mass index alone.

tf.s: Most people with pre-clinical obesity ended up with clinical obesity.
tf.why: Most of them, 77 to 91 percent, did not end up with clinical obesity within 10 years.

tf.s: In clinical obesity, extra body fat is already harming the organs.
tf.why: The method breaks obesity down into two levels, and only in clinical obesity are the organs already harmed.

tf.s: The new method leaves out the body mass index and uses only the waist.
tf.why: It keeps the body mass index and adds waist measurements, because the index alone leaves out where fat sits.

lines.text: Did you see that story about obesity and waist size?
I did. [[Out of curiosity]], what's wrong with the body mass index?
It's only weight and height. It {{leaves out}} where your fat is.
So a guy with a lot of muscle could get a high number?
Right. The number alone can't {{tell those people apart}}.
[[How come]] the waist matters so much?
Experts say fat that {{builds up}} around the belly is linked to more health problems.
Who {{came up with}} the new method?
An international group of obesity experts, in January 2025. Now a big study {{backs it up}}.
Researchers {{looked into}} how well it works, with the records of more than 840,000 adults in four countries.
And the old number made mistakes?
It didn't {{pick up}} obesity in as many as 9 percent of people. That can {{add up to}} tens of millions.
So does a big waist mean you're sick?
[[Not necessarily]]. Most people with pre-clinical obesity didn't {{end up}} with clinical obesity after 10 years.
[[That's reassuring]]. But I guess doctors shouldn't {{brush it off}} either.
Exactly. The researchers say doctors should treat it [[case by case]].

expressions.def: Used before a question to show you simply want to know the answer
ex: Out of curiosity, how much did your new bike cost?
Out of curiosity, where did you learn to cook like this?

expressions.def: Used to ask why something happens or is true
ex: How come the store is closed today?
How come you never drink coffee?

expressions.def: Used to say that something is not always true
ex: Expensive shoes are not necessarily better.
A long line doesn't necessarily mean the food is good.

expressions.def: Used to say that some news makes you feel less worried
ex: The doctor said it's nothing serious. That's reassuring.
The bridge was checked last month? That's reassuring.

expressions.def: Judging each person or situation separately, not all the same way
ex: The school decides about late homework case by case.
The bank checks each loan request case by case.
